title: The Dassler Brothers Split a Town in Two
text:
In 1924 Adolf and Rudolf Dassler founded a shoe company in their small Bavarian hometown of Herzogenaurach. Adolf, known as Adi, was the quiet craftsman who designed the shoes; Rudolf was the outgoing salesman. Their spiked running shoes became famous when Jesse Owens wore them at the Berlin Olympics of 1936.

During the Second World War the brothers and their wives, who lived in the same house, grew bitter toward one another. Rudolf was drafted, and later came to believe that Adi had a hand in it. After the war Rudolf was held by the Americans and suspected his brother had denounced him. The details of who said what are disputed, but the resentment was real and lasting.

In 1948 they split the company. Rudolf set up his own firm on the other side of the little Aurach river, which became Puma. Adi named his business after himself: Adidas. The two companies became fierce rivals, and the town divided with them. Workers of each firm used different bakeries, pubs and shops, and Herzogenaurach was nicknamed "the town of bent necks" because people looked at your shoes before speaking to you.

The brothers never reconciled. When they died, Rudolf in 1974 and Adi in 1978, they were buried in the same cemetery, at opposite ends. Only in 2009 did employees of the two companies play a friendly football match together.
lesson: A family quarrel left unresolved can outlive everyone in it and divide whole communities. Repair is easiest early, before pride hardens into identity.
source: Barbara Smit, Sneaker Wars (2008); company histories of Adidas and Puma
caveat: The exact causes of the brothers' quarrel are disputed and partly based on family accounts.
